name: Saint Lawrence Ruiz and Companions, Martyrs
alternateNames: Saint Thomas Nishi and Fifteen Companions
briefBio: Lawrence Ruiz and fifteen companions were lay women and men, religious, catechists, interpreters, and priests from Japan, the Philippines, Europe, and mixed communities linked through Manila. They were killed under Tokugawa repression in 1633–1637. Lawrence was a married father from Binondo of Chinese and Tagala parentage; he joined a 1636 Dominican party amid an unresolved accusation, not a planned search for martyrdom. Near-contemporary Dominican reports preserve valuable testimony through a partisan lens. Their collective memorial rejects torture, colonial triumphalism, nationalist possession, and contempt for Japanese people or religions.

editorial.reviewer: Catholic Daily factual and theological review

whyItMatters: This memorial belongs to all sixteen witnesses, not to one nationality. It joins fidelity with historical honesty about coercion, colonial networks, fear, migration, and companion agency, while refusing to shame people who seek safety or break under torture.
oneMinuteSummary: Lawrence Ruiz and fifteen companions were lay women and men, catechists, an interpreter-guide, religious brothers, and priests connected across Japan, Manila, Taiwan, and Europe. Nine of Lawrence's companions were Japanese. They were killed under Tokugawa repression in 1633, 1634, and 1637. Lawrence was a married father from Binondo with a Chinese father and Tagala mother. He joined a 1636 Dominican party amid an unresolved violent accusation; he did not leave home seeking death. A 1638 Dominican relation is close to events but partisan and mediated, while later formal sources preserve the roster. State anxiety about Iberian trade, mission, and colonial power helps explain policy but cannot justify torture or execution. Their witness must not fuel anti-Japanese hostility, Philippine ownership, or Spanish missionary triumphalism. Apostasy under torture is not shameful. People facing persecution may flee, protect dependants, seek asylum and legal help, and receive trauma-informed care.

sections.heading: Sixteen distinct witnesses
sections.body: Formal beatification and canonization sources define sixteen witnesses, nine of them Japanese, alongside Filipino, mixed Chinese-Tagala, Spanish, French, and Italian companions: women and men, lay and ordained, married and religious, catechists and an interpreter.

sections.heading: Roster and title across reception
sections.body: Hornedo's 1980 pre-beatification review discussed Villarroel's seventeen-person book roster, including ten Japanese, and questioned Lawrence's title prominence. The later formal sixteen-person group, with nine Japanese companions, is therefore controlled by the 1981 and 1987 Holy See sources rather than that review.

sections.heading: Lawrence's path from Binondo
sections.body: Lawrence was a married father formed in Binondo. He entered the 1636 party amid an obscure violent incident or accusation; reviewed sources do not establish guilt or innocence, and his departure was not a deliberate search for martyrdom.

sections.heading: Trial under coercive policy
sections.body: A near-contemporary Dominican relation and later formal records describe arrest, trial, forced apostasy, and killing. Tokugawa repression developed amid mission, trade, and colonial anxieties; that context neither makes Japanese society inherently hostile nor justifies torture.

sections.heading: Courage without shame or nationalism
sections.body: Some companions faltered under torture and returned to their profession of faith. Such accounts cannot shame survivors. The collective memory resists reducing Japanese companions to a Filipino hero's background or turning canonization into national or colonial possession.

life.gospelTheme: Christ gathers witnesses across peoples and vocations, sustaining fidelity while condemning torture, coercion, and domination.
life.struggle: Martyr stories can erase companions, glorify exposure, shame coerced apostasy, or become weapons of nationalism and hostility.
life.response: Remember every companion, name coercion truthfully, reject ethnic blame, and protect threatened people through safe, lawful, trauma-informed support.

virtues.name: Companion solidarity
virtues.evidence: The formal group spans cultures, genders, family states, ministries, exile, disability, and migration.
virtues.imitation: Tell a shared story by naming overlooked contributors and letting affected people define their own agency.

virtues.name: Faith under coercion
virtues.evidence: Sources preserve resistance and also temporary apostasy under deliberately engineered torture.
virtues.imitation: Support a threatened person without demanding confrontation, disclosure, or heroic performance.

practice.spiritual: Pray Romans 8:35–39 for persecuted communities and for people whose bodies or speech are controlled by violence.
practice.action: Learn a confidential legal, asylum, safeguarding, or trauma-care referral route; never publish a threatened person's identity or location without informed consent.

reflectionQuestions: Whose agency disappears when I tell this as Lawrence's story alone?
Do I mistake danger-seeking or nationalist pride for faithful witness?

scripture.connection: Paul names severe pressures without declaring violence good; God's love holds persons whom coercion tries to isolate.

prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, unite us with Saint Lawrence Ruiz and all his companions. Protect people under coercion, strengthen families and exiles, heal those marked by torture, and free our memory from nationalism and contempt. Give us courage joined to prudent safety, solidarity, and peace. Amen.
